analysis.one_liner: Gives people court access to sue over violations of COVID relief and employment laws, and pauses forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 14 Democratic cosponsors in May 2020, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let individuals sue in federal court against anyone who violated the CARES Act or the Families First Coronavirus Response Act and harmed them — for example, an employer that failed to pay required pandemic leave or a company that misused relief rules. It would also make predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes during the COVID emergency and 180 days after it ends, so workers and consumers could take claims to court instead of being pushed into private, company-chosen arbitration. Voluntary arbitration after a dispute arises would still be allowed, and union contracts would keep their arbitration provisions.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, consumers, and civil rights plaintiffs. Employees (including independent contractors) with claims about pay, discipline, or discrimination during the pandemic could go to court instead of being bound by arbitration clauses they signed before any dispute existed. Consumers injured by companies that violated COVID relief rules would get a direct right to sue. Groups seeking class actions on antitrust or civil rights claims could not be blocked by blanket class-action waivers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, consumers, and class action plaintiffs

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federal cause of action letting individuals sue in U.S. district court against any person who violated or failed to comply with the CARES Act or the Families First Coronavirus Response Act, for harm they suffered as a result.

During the COVID emergency period and 180 days after it ends, predispute arbitration agreements and predispute joint-action (class or collective action) waivers would be unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes.
A court, not an arbitrator, would decide whether the suspension applies, even if the contract tries to delegate that question to an arbitrator.

The bill covers independent contractors as well as employees and preserves the right to seek judicial enforcement of constitutional, statutory, or public-policy rights even where a union contract has arbitration.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and employers. Companies facing claims would lose the ability to force workers and consumers into individual arbitration and would face new lawsuit exposure under the COVID relief laws at a time when many were struggling with the pandemic and fast-moving compliance rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill would override arbitration agreements already signed before the emergency began, unsettling contracts made under existing federal arbitration law; businesses operating under pre-pandemic agreements would face disputes handled outside the forum they had bargained for.

A blanket right to sue over any CARES Act or Families First violation could generate a wave of litigation against businesses already stressed by the pandemic and by rapidly changing compliance requirements, which small employers in particular would have found hard to absorb.

The suspension is temporary and covers only four categories of disputes, so after the covered period ends the existing arbitration system would return unchanged; critics would say this creates uncertainty without lasting reform.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and consumers, the benefits are real and time-limited: court access during a period when many lost jobs, wages, or paid leave protections. The costs fall on employers and consumer-facing businesses in the form of litigation exposure and the loss of forced arbitration during the covered period. Honest tradeoffs exist — litigation is slower and more expensive than arbitration for many individual claims, and a new federal cause of action adds compliance risk during a crisis — but the bill was designed narrowly (voluntary post-dispute arbitration still allowed, union contracts largely preserved) and it never got far enough for those tradeoffs to be weighed by any committee or floor vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the same day in May 2020, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on May 26, 2020, with Reps. Takano, Garcia of Illinois, and Cartwright as original cosponsors.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced.
The bill attracted 14 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further legislative action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the record before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and businesses that use predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers kept their existing rights to channel employment, consumer, and civil rights disputes into individual arbitration, and faced no new private lawsuit exposure under the COVID relief laws.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers keeping forced arbitration and class waivers

for.name: Rep. Janice D. Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a right to sue over COVID relief law violations and suspend forced arbitration during the pandemic emergency.

for.name: 14 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans joined.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Jerrold Nadler, D)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat after referral until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor in the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 supporters were House Democrats — the sponsor plus 14 cosponsors — and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never advanced past referral, so no votes were ever recorded.

industries.industry: Employers using forced arbitration (staffing firms, gig platforms, retail and service chains)
industries.note: The bill would have made predispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers unenforceable in employment disputes during the covered period, letting workers (including independent contractors) take pay, discipline, and discrimination claims to court. Its death left those clauses fully enforceable.

industries.industry: Consumer-facing businesses and financial firms using consumer arbitration clauses
industries.note: Consumer and antitrust disputes could not be forced into individual arbitration during the covered period, and the bill's new cause of action would have given consumers a direct right to sue over CARES Act violations. Blocking the bill preserved the status quo, in which consumers typically must arbitrate individually.

industries.industry: Companies that received or administered COVID relief
industries.note: The bill would have created private lawsuits for harms from any CARES Act or Families First violation, adding litigation exposure on top of federal enforcement. Without the bill, accountability for those violations rests only with government agencies.

The bill mostly preserves arbitration in collective bargaining agreements, but would stop such clauses from waiving a worker's right to go to court to enforce constitutional, statutory, or public-policy rights.
